encounters.source: NASA/JPL (classic, pre-Gaia): JPL Voyager 'Interstellar Mission' page (now offline; widely quoted): 'within 1.6 light years ... of AC+79 3888' in ~40,000 yr. NASA image article 'Reaching for the Stars' (2013-09-11) gives 1.7 ly.
NASA/JPL (classic, pre-Gaia): NASA/JPL Photojournal PIA22921 caption and JPL interstellar mission page: ~1.7 ly from Ross 248 in ~40,000 yr.

notes: Gliese 445 does most of the travelling: it is falling toward the Sun at ~111 km/s (Gaia DR3 RV) while Voyager 1 recedes at 16.6 km/s. In ~44,000 yr the star itself passes ~1.0 pc (3.3 ly) from the Sun (our linear model; see bodies[].closest_to_sun_linear).

Gaia-era distances (Bailer-Jones & Farnocchia 2019): V1-Gliese 445 0.575 pc = 1.88 ly at 44.0 kyr; V2-Ross 248 0.529 pc = 1.73 ly at 42.0 kyr. NASA's classic 1.6 / 1.7 ly at ~40 kyr are close; V1's is ~0.3 ly too small.
Neither flyby is Voyager's closest. With Gaia DR2, V1's closest known star is TYC 3135-52-1 (0.30 pc, ~303 kyr; possibly binary) and Proxima Centauri comes first for both craft (~1 pc at 17-20 kyr).

Our straight-line model (Gaia DR3, no Galactic gravity) reproduces Bailer-Jones & Farnocchia (Gaia DR2, Galactic potential) to <1% in distance and time for both flybys: over ~40 kyr these nearby stars barely feel the Galaxy, and the remaining differences are mostly DR2 -> DR3 astrometry.

The craft's r0 is its baked position on the epoch; the velocity is the asymptote (the craft are still slowing by ~0.3 km/s, a positional error of a few hundred au over 40 kyr, negligible against ~1e5 au).
